message.content:
When choosing a rock for a garden sculpture, you’ll want something that balances durability, workability, and visual appeal. Here are the top options: | Rock | Why it’s good for garden sculptures | Typical uses | |------|-------------------------------------|--------------| | **Marble** | • Strong yet workable when freshly quarried.
• Weather‑resistant once finished.
• Classic look that ages beautifully. | Classical statues, fountains, decorative columns. | | **Granite** | • Extremely hard and long‑lasting.
• Holds fine detail well when polished.
• Resistant to freeze‑thaw cycles. | Large outdoor monuments, stone benches, retaining walls. | | **Sandstone** | • Easier to carve than granite or marble.
• Porous but can be sealed for protection.
• Warm, earthy tones. | Garden benches, low relief panels, rustic sculptures. | | **Limestone** | • Softer than granite, easier to shape.
• Holds detail nicely when freshly cut.
• Can weather to a subtle patina. | Low‑relief bas-reliefs, garden edging, small statues. | | **Travertine** | • Porous but durable once sealed.
• Unique veining adds texture.
• Good for outdoor use if properly treated. | Water features, garden walls, decorative accents. | ### Quick recommendation - **For a classic, timeless look**: Marble (especially Carrara or Calacatta). - **For maximum durability**: Granite (e.g., Gabbro or Tonalite). - **For a more affordable, still‑durable option**: Sandstone or limestone, especially if you seal it. If you’re planning a specific style or have a particular climate in mind, let me know and I can narrow down the best choice for your project!
